nodes.label: Load Balancer
nodes.about: Spreads requests across the app servers in turn (round robin) and skips servers that are down.
nodes.when_down: Nothing gets in: every request fails with 502. This is why real load balancers run as a redundant pair.

nodes.label: App Server 1
nodes.about: Runs the product API. Stateless, so any server can answer any request.
nodes.when_down: The load balancer sends everything to App Server 2. Users notice nothing.

nodes.label: App Server 2
nodes.about: A second copy of the product API, in another zone.
nodes.when_down: The load balancer sends everything to App Server 1.

nodes.label: Redis
nodes.about: Keeps recently read products in memory (cache-aside): a hit takes 1 ms instead of 30 ms.
nodes.when_down: Reads fall through to Postgres, so pages get slower and the database takes the full load. When Redis comes back it is empty and has to warm up again.

nodes.label: Postgres
nodes.about: The source of truth for products.
nodes.when_down: Cached products still load; anything not in Redis fails with 502, and updates fail.

update_product.say: Invalidate the cached copy so the next read sees the change

scenarios.label: Cache hit
scenarios.explain: The first read stored product 7 in Redis, so this one never touches Postgres: about 4 ms instead of 35 ms.

scenarios.label: Redis is down
scenarios.explain: Cache-aside degrades gracefully: the app skips the cache and reads Postgres. Slower, but it still works.

scenarios.label: Zone A outage
scenarios.explain: Running servers in two zones means losing a whole zone costs capacity, not availability.

scenarios.label: Postgres down, warm cache
scenarios.explain: Products already in Redis keep loading while the database is down. Try a key you haven't read yet: it fails.

scenarios.label: Postgres down, cold cache
scenarios.explain: Nothing is cached, so the read has to reach Postgres, and it can't.
